client: I've been having a really hard time since my brother passed away six months ago. It was a car accident, completely out of nowhere, and ever since then I just... can't seem to enjoy being around people the way I used to. I show up to things with friends and I just feel hollow inside, like I'm going through the motions, and honestly I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change any of that.
therapist: What you've been carrying since losing your brother so suddenly sounds incredibly heavy, and that sense of going through the motions — feeling hollow even when you're surrounded by people you care about — is such a real and painful part of grief. I also notice that as you're describing all of this, there's an energy in how you're speaking that makes me curious — almost like part of you is working very hard right now, maybe to hold something together or to get through saying it. I wonder, what does it feel like in your body as you're talking about this?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, there's this tightness in my chest, like something is just sitting there and won't move. And my jaw feels clenched, I didn't even notice that until you asked. I guess I'm used to just pushing through it and not really paying attention to what's happening in my body.
therapist: That tightness in your chest and the clenched jaw — your body has been quietly holding so much, even when your mind was focused on just getting through the day. It takes real courage to slow down and actually listen to what's happening inside, especially when pushing through has felt like the only way to survive these past six months. I'm curious — when you notice that tightness right now, is there a feeling or even a word that seems to live underneath it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: If I really sit with it... I think the word is "guilty." Like, I keep coming back to this feeling that I should have called him more, should have made more plans with him, and now I just can't stop thinking about all the things I never said. It's easier to feel that tightness than to actually name it, because naming it makes it feel more real.
therapist: Naming it as guilt took real courage, and it makes so much sense that putting a word to it feels almost dangerous — like saying it out loud makes the loss more final and undeniable. What I'm noticing is that even as you're sharing something so painful, your voice sounds almost careful, like you're trying to hold it very gently, maybe to keep it from overwhelming you. I wonder — when you imagine what you might have said to your brother if you'd had the chance, what feels most important?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think I just would have wanted him to know that I was proud of him, and that I loved him, and that I didn't take for granted that he'd always be there. But even saying that now feels almost pointless, like what good does it do to know what I would have said when I can't actually say it. I don't know, maybe that's where I get stuck, because it feels like sitting with any of this just leads to a dead end.
therapist: What you just said — that you wanted him to know you were proud of him and loved him — that's not pointless at all, because it tells you something true and important about who you are as a brother and what that relationship meant to you. I notice that even as you're describing feeling stuck, something in how you're speaking sounds almost quieter, more tender, like part of you is being very gentle with this. I'm wondering if the "dead end" feeling might actually be grief protecting you from sitting too long in something that feels unbearable — and whether, slowly, there might be a way to let those words you never got to say still mean something, even now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that, but I honestly don't know how those words can mean something when there's no one to receive them. Like, who are they for at this point? I guess I'm skeptical that finding some way to "honor" what I felt is going to actually make this hollow feeling go away when I'm sitting with friends and just feeling completely alone.
therapist: Your skepticism makes complete sense, and I don't want to offer you something that feels hollow or like a platitude — you deserve more than that. What strikes me is that the loneliness you're describing with friends, that feeling of being surrounded by people and still completely alone, sounds like one of the most painful parts of all of this, maybe even more than the grief itself. I'm curious — is there anyone in your life right now who you feel even a little less alone with, or has this feeling of distance settled in everywhere?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: There's maybe one person, my friend Dana, who knew my brother too, and sometimes when we're together there's this brief moment where it feels like she actually gets it without me having to explain everything. But even with her I hold back a lot, because I don't want to keep being the person who brings the mood down or makes everything heavy. I guess I've been telling myself that people can only take so much of someone else's grief before they start pulling away.
therapist: What you have with Dana sounds genuinely precious — those moments where you don't have to translate your grief for someone, where she just *knows*, because she loved him too. And I notice that even as you're describing her, your voice gets very soft, almost careful, like you're holding this connection gently because it matters so much. I wonder if the belief that people will pull away if you show too much is something grief taught you as a way to protect yourself — and whether Dana has actually given you any signs that she's reaching her limit, or if that might be a fear rather than a fact?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, when I think about it, Dana hasn't actually pulled away at all — she still checks in on me, she still brings up my brother's name like it's okay to say it out loud, which most people don't do. But knowing that doesn't automatically make the fear go away, because I think it's less about what Dana has actually done and more about this deeper worry that eventually everyone has a limit and I'll hit it. It's like I know logically you might be right, but emotionally I'm still bracing for it to happen.
therapist: You just did something really important — you separated what the evidence actually shows from what the fear tells you, and that distinction is at the heart of so much of what keeps us stuck in pain. That bracing feeling, waiting for people to hit their limit, sounds like it might have a longer history than just these six months — like grief may have activated something that was already quietly there. I'm curious, does that fear of eventually being "too much" for people feel familiar to you from before you lost your brother?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, if I'm being honest, that fear has been around a lot longer than six months. Even growing up I had this sense that I needed to manage how much of myself I showed people, like there was a version of me that was acceptable and a version that was too needy or too sad or too much. I guess I just never really connected that to what's happening now, and it's a little unsettling to think that losing my brother might have just turned up the volume on something I've been carrying for a really long time.
therapist: What you just connected is really significant — that this fear of being "too much" isn't a new wound grief created, but an old one that loss made impossible to keep quiet anymore. And I notice that even as you're saying something so vulnerable and true about yourself, your voice is very soft, almost like you're speaking carefully, as if this realization is both important and a little fragile right now. It makes me want to ask — what's it like to see that younger version of you, the one who learned to manage how much they showed, with the same compassion you might offer someone else who had carried that for so long?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: It's hard, because when I try to look at that younger version of me with compassion, there's this immediate voice that says he should have just been tougher, like the managing and the holding back was a weakness rather than something he learned to do to survive. I can extend compassion to other people pretty easily, but when I turn it toward myself it feels almost undeserved, like I haven't earned the right to be gentle with myself when my brother is the one who actually lost everything. I guess that's where the guilt and the self-compassion kind of crash into each other.
therapist: The way you just put that — that your brother is the one who "actually lost everything" — that's such a painful and revealing thought, because it shows how grief and guilt have quietly convinced you that you don't have the right to your own suffering. But I want to gently offer this: the boy who learned to hold back and manage wasn't weak, he was doing the only thing he knew how to do to stay connected to people he loved — and that's exactly what you're still doing now, even with your brother gone. What do you think he would say, if he could, about whether you've earned the right to be gentle with yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That question kind of stops me, because I know, I really do know, that he would have hated seeing me punish myself like this. He was always the one telling me to stop being so hard on myself, actually, which makes it almost cruel that I'm doing exactly that in response to losing him. I guess part of me just doesn't fully trust that knowing what he'd say is enough to actually change how I feel about myself.
therapist: There's something almost unbearably poignant in what you just shared — that the person who always told you to stop being so hard on yourself is the very one you're grieving, like losing him also meant losing that voice of gentleness from outside you. And I notice something tender in how you're speaking right now, very soft, like this realization is landing somewhere deep and real. You're right that knowing isn't the same as feeling — but I wonder if part of the work ahead is slowly learning to carry that voice of his *inside* you, not as a way to replace the grief, but as a way of letting him still be present in how you treat yourself.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
